title: #CetaphilCalledMeOut: Behavior-Led Brand Strategy
summary: A PM-level strategy case study for Cetaphil: moving from skincare awareness to habit formation through a 7-day behavior-led experience.

strategySlides.label: 01 Problem
strategySlides.title: Inconsistent product outcomes
strategySlides.text: Reviews split between gentle results and irritation — same product, very different experiences.

strategySlides.label: 02 Insight
strategySlides.title: The gap is behavior, not the product
strategySlides.text: Users switch, overuse, and quit before consistency has a chance to work.

strategySlides.label: 03 Action
strategySlides.title: Train Your Skin — 7 Days
strategySlides.text: A guided loop: log behavior → get feedback → build habit → unlock your personalized call-out.

content.text: The product isn't failing. The usage is.

This is the complete strategy behind Episode 01 of #IFIRANTHEBRAND. The reel introduces the idea in 60 seconds. This case study unpacks it at a product-management level: what I observed in real user behavior, what insight explains it, what product experience could solve it, and how the campaign turns that experience into a shareable brand moment.
1. The Observation That Started This

While studying Cetaphil reviews across Amazon, Reddit, and skincare communities, I noticed a clear and repeating pattern. The same product was creating very different outcomes for different users — some calling it a holy grail, others reporting breakouts, irritation, or zero results. What was causing the split? Not the formula. The behavior.

content.label: Real words from real users
voices: I used it for a few days but saw no result.
I don't know if I'm using too much or too little.
My skin reacts differently every week.
I keep switching products every time something doesn't work instantly.
I blamed the product. Turns out I was the problem.

content.label: Core PM Insight
content.text: The gap is not awareness. The gap is behavior. Most users already know Cetaphil. They just don't know how to use it consistently — and no one is helping them figure that out.
2. Who Is Actually Struggling?

users.title: The Confused Skincare Beginner
traits: "I don't know what works for my skin"
Switches products after 3–4 days with no results
Uses too much product hoping for faster results
Never gives a routine enough time to judge it fairly
Blames the product before examining the behavior

users.title: The Sensitive Skin User
traits: Scared of irritation and unexpected breakouts
Wants reassurance that they're doing it right
Stops at the first sign of dryness or change
Needs someone to say: your skin is adjusting, not reacting
Looking for confidence, not just a cleanser

content.text: 3. The Strategic Opportunity

Cetaphil already has a skin analysis tool — useful for discovery, but it behaves like a one-time snapshot. It tells users about their skin type. It doesn't guide daily behavior, habit formation, or routine consistency. That's the gap. The opportunity is to move from analysis to action.

content.alt: Behavior comparison — current vs proposed skincare experience
content.caption: Current experience: buy → use alone → get uncertain results → blame product. Proposed: buy → enter guided journey → log behavior → understand skin → build trust.

content.text: 4. Product Concept: Train Your Skin

A guided, interactive 7-day skincare experience that helps users understand how their own behavior affects their skin results. It's not a promotional campaign. It's a behavior-tracking product layer that turns inconsistent usage into a simple daily feedback loop — and ends with a personalized, shareable moment.

steps.title: Scan & Enter
steps.text: QR code on packaging, trial kits, influencer posts, or e-commerce inserts. Zero friction — no app download required.

steps.title: Skin Onboarding
steps.text: 3 quick questions: skin type, main concern, current routine. Builds a behavioral baseline before Day 1 begins.

steps.title: Daily 10-Second Check-In
steps.text: Did you use it? How much? Which products did you combine? How does your skin feel today? Light enough to actually do every day.

steps.title: Real-Time Feedback
steps.text: The system reads behavior and explains what the routine is actually doing. Skip 2 days? It tells you why that matters. Overused it? It explains the irritation.

steps.title: Dynamic Skin Avatar
steps.text: A visual avatar that updates daily based on logged behavior. Consistent use → calm, stable skin. Product switching → confused skin state. Makes the invisible visible.

steps.title: Day 7 Personalized Call-Out
steps.text: The campaign moment. The Cetaphil bottle reflects the user's 7-day behavior back to them — honest, playful, shareable. This is where the experience becomes a story worth posting.

content.text: 5. The Day 7 Moment

At the end of 7 days, users unlock a personalized message generated from their actual behavior log. The tone is warm and direct — not judgmental, not fake-positive. It mirrors what the user actually did and gives them a reason to share it.

content.label: Day 7 Call-Out Examples
content.headline: Your bottle has something to say.
examples: I didn't fail you. You skipped me 3 nights in a row.
You changed products 4 times this week. Your skin was confused, not broken.
You used too much product twice. Gentle skin needs gentle usage.
You were consistent, patient, and gentle. That's exactly why your skin felt calmer.
You showed up 6 out of 7 days. Your skin noticed.

content.alt: Cetaphil Day 7 truth reveal — behavior call-out card
content.caption: The reveal card turns 7 days of behavior into one clear, personal, shareable moment.

content.text: 6. The Product Loops

items: Behavior Loop — Log usage → receive feedback → improve routine → see better stability → continue.
Habit Loop — Daily check-in → streak maintained → points earned → reward unlocked → user returns.
Social Loop — Complete 7 days → receive personalized call-out → share it → friends join the challenge.
Commerce Loop — Start with trial kit → follow guided routine → gain confidence → redeem discount → buy full size.

content.text: 7. MVP — What I Would Build First
Not a full app. A mobile-first web prototype — no downloads, works from a QR scan. Speed to test matters more than completeness at this stage.

content.text: 8. Success Metrics

content.north-star-why: If a user completes all 7 check-ins, the behavior habit is forming. Every downstream metric — sharing, trust, conversion, retention — flows from this single signal.

content.text: 9. Go-To-Market: 4 Phases

phases.title: Prototype Test
phases.text: Small user group. Validate: does the onboarding feel clear? Do check-ins feel easy? Does the Day 7 call-out feel shareable enough to post?

phases.title: Trial Kit Launch
phases.text: 7-Day Train Your Skin Kit — trial-size product + QR code + simple instructions + challenge access + reward at completion. Helps users try the product the right way.

phases.title: Creator-Led Challenge
phases.text: Creators document their 7-day journey. Day 1: 'Starting the challenge.' Day 3: 'Used too much — here's what happened.' Day 7: 'Cetaphil just called me out.' The call-out card becomes the viral moment.

phases.title: Social Sharing Wave
phases.text: Users share their own Day 7 cards. 'I blamed the product. Turns out I was the problem.' The campaign is relatable because the behavior gap is universal.

content.caption: One personal story becomes a participation format. The social loop scales without paid distribution.

content.text: 10. Why This Strategy Works

items: It solves a real problem — inconsistent outcomes caused by inconsistent behavior.
It creates value before asking for loyalty — users learn something before they're sold to.
It turns the reveal moment into earned media — the call-out card is shareable because it feels personal and relatable.
It reduces negative perception — users understand their own role in the outcome instead of blaming the product.
It builds retention through habit — 7 days of check-ins creates routine ownership, not just brand awareness.

content.text: Instead of saying the product works — we help it work for the user.

title: Not Handwash: Packaging-Led Behavior Strategy
summary: A PM-level strategy case study for Cetaphil: redesigning packaging perception, refill behavior, travel usability, and sustainability around a premium skincare system.

strategySlides.label: 01 Problem
strategySlides.title: Real packaging friction
strategySlides.text: Users trust the formula, but the pack feels less premium.

strategySlides.label: 02 Insight
strategySlides.title: Packaging shapes perceived value
strategySlides.text: Basic packaging makes skincare feel like utility.

strategySlides.label: 03 Action
strategySlides.title: Build a refillable premium system
strategySlides.text: Make Cetaphil reusable, refillable, and travel-safe.

content.text: NOT HANDWASH. If the formula is dermatologist-trusted, the packaging should say the same.

This is the complete strategy behind Episode 02 of #IFIRANTHEBRAND. The reel frames the question in 60 seconds — why does a trusted skincare brand still have packaging that could pass for handwash? This case study unpacks the product-management answer: what users are actually experiencing, what behavior is being shaped by the wrong packaging signals, and how a redesigned, refillable system changes everything from first impression to repeat purchase.
1. Executive Summary

Cetaphil's formula has decades of dermatologist trust and a loyal global user base. But the packaging — functional, clinical, and simple — creates a perception gap that directly affects user behavior. When users see the bottle on a sink, they treat it like utility skincare. They leave it in the bathroom instead of their deliberate routine. They skip it while traveling because the pump leaks. They throw the bottle away without thinking. The opportunity is not just to make the bottle prettier. It is to redesign the entire system around behavior: how users use it, store it, travel with it, refill it, and emotionally relate to it. This strategy proposes a refillable premium packaging system anchored by the campaign line: Not Handwash.
2. Problem Statement

Cetaphil has strong category credibility. But when a premium skincare brand's bottle visually blends into the bathroom sink alongside bodywash, handwash, and cleaning products, the packaging is working against the product. The current design communicates utility, not skincare. Clinical, not intentional. Accessible, but not worth pausing for. And packaging — before the product is ever used — sets the behavioral expectations that shape how users engage with what is inside.

content.label: Core PM Insight
content.text: Design controls behavior. If a product looks like handwash, people treat it like handwash. Packaging is not just aesthetic — it is a product decision that shapes usage, storage, travel behavior, emotional attachment, and repeat purchase.
3. Why Packaging Is a Product Problem, Not a Design Problem

A PM does not think of packaging as the outer shell. Packaging is the first touch in the product experience. It sets expectations before a single drop of cleanser reaches skin. When packaging does not match the quality of the formula inside, four things go wrong. Users do not place the product intentionally — they grab it out of habit, not from a deliberate routine. Users do not feel emotionally attached — the bottle is a container, not a ritual object. Users do not travel with it — leaks and inconvenience mean the routine breaks the moment life gets busier. And users do not refill or repurchase proactively — they wait until they run out because the product does not feel worth maintaining.
4. User Pain Points

content.label: Real friction from real users
voices: Honestly it looks like handwash. I had to check the label twice before I bought it.
The pump leaked all over my bag during my flight. I don't travel with it anymore.
I use it but it doesn't feel like a skincare product. It's just there on the sink.
I feel bad throwing the bottle away every month but there's no refill option.
I ran out and didn't notice for a week. It doesn't feel essential enough to track.

content.text: 5. Target Users

users.title: The Skincare Routinist
traits: Already trusts Cetaphil but wants the experience to match the quality
Places premium products prominently — on the counter, not under the sink
Would pay slightly more for a bottle they are proud to keep and display
Dislikes wasting product and wants a smarter, cleaner pump mechanism
Shares products they consider beautiful or intentional on social media

users.title: The Sustainability-Conscious Millennial
traits: Feels guilt every time they throw away a plastic pump bottle
Actively looks for refillable alternatives in personal care
Will switch to a brand that has a credible and convenient sustainability story
Wants eco-friendly and convenient — not one at the expense of the other
Responds well to brands that make sustainable behavior feel effortless and visible

users.title: The Frequent Traveler
traits: Has had cleanser leak on clothes, bags, and other products
Wants a travel-safe pump that does not require decanting into tiny bottles
Buys travel-size versions repeatedly rather than carrying the full size
Would love a full-size bottle that is genuinely travel-ready out of the box
Values thoughtful design that solves real-world friction, not just aesthetics

content.text: 6. Strategic Opportunity

Cetaphil already has the hardest thing to build: trust. Millions of users know the formula works. The strategic opportunity is not to win new trust but to extend existing trust into the full product experience — the packaging, the refill system, the digital touchpoint, and the emotional story around the bottle. Moving from a disposable clinical bottle to a premium refillable skincare system is not just a design change. It is a behavior change. And behavior changes drive retention, repeat purchase, and brand equity in ways that campaigns alone cannot.

content.caption: A system reframe: from clinical utility bottle to intentional skincare object with a refillable life cycle.

content.text: 7. Proposed Solution: The Refill UX System
The formula stays the same. The system around it earns premium status.

The Cetaphil Refill UX System is a three-layer product redesign. Layer one is the packaging — a new bottle silhouette, finish, and mechanism. Layer two is the refill infrastructure — pouches, QR reorder flow, and subscribe-and-save. Layer three is the digital touchpoint — the QR experience that connects users to their routine, refill, and skin education in one place. Together, these three layers turn a one-time purchase into an ongoing skin system.
8. Packaging Redesign: 5 Core Features

steps.title: Premium Bottle Silhouette
steps.text: A slimmer, taller, more intentional shape that communicates skincare, not utility. The bottle should look like it belongs on a bathroom counter alongside serums — not next to soap dispensers and cleaning products.

steps.title: Airless Pump with Travel Lock
steps.text: An airless pump mechanism that eliminates leakage and preserves the formula from air exposure. A built-in lock for travel means users never have to decant again — one bottle, every environment, zero spills.

steps.title: Matte Soft-Touch Finish
steps.text: A matte exterior finish that changes the tactile experience of using the product. Soft-touch materials feel premium in the hand, which changes how users think about and treat the product they are holding.

steps.title: Pastel Color Variants
steps.text: Soft, skin-tone-adjacent pastel variants — not replacements for the signature Cetaphil look, but collectible editions. Makes the bottle desirable to display, to gift, and to keep rather than discard after one use.

steps.title: Refill Indicator Window
steps.text: A small level indicator on the side of the bottle lets users see when they are running low. Reduces the 'I ran out and didn't notice' failure mode and prompts timely refill reorders before the routine breaks.

content.text: 9. The Refill System

content.alt: Cetaphil refill journey — pouch, QR scan, and subscription flow
content.caption: The refill journey: scan the QR, order the pouch, subscribe, and never run out again.

content.text: The hero bottle is the anchor. The refill pouch is the engine. Users buy the premium bottle once and refill through biodegradable, minimal-plastic pouches that contain the same Cetaphil formula. The pouch reduces packaging waste, simplifies reorder logistics, and signals a sustainability commitment without sacrificing convenience.

items: Reusable hero bottle designed to last 2+ years as the owned skincare object.
Biodegradable refill pouches — lower plastic footprint, lower cost, same trusted formula.
QR code on the bottle triggers a complete refill order in under 60 seconds.
Subscribe-and-save model: users set a delivery cadence and receive a loyalty discount.
Sustainability dashboard on the digital experience shows plastic saved per refill cycle.

content.text: 10. Digital Experience Flow

steps.title: QR Scan on Bottle
steps.text: Every Cetaphil bottle carries a QR code. One scan from any phone camera. No app download, no account creation required at entry. Instant access to the full digital experience in under 3 seconds.

steps.title: Registration & Skin Setup
steps.text: New users answer three quick questions: skin type, primary concern, and current routine. Returns a personalised usage guide and sets the baseline for future product recommendations and refill timing.

steps.title: Usage Education
steps.text: An animated micro-guide shows how to use the airless pump correctly — the right amount, the right technique, morning versus night. Reduces misuse and irritation before it creates dissatisfaction with the formula.

steps.title: Refill Indicator Check
steps.text: The experience reads the user's registration date and estimated usage pace to flag when they may be running low. A smart low-stock prompt — not a generic marketing push — based on actual behaviour data.

steps.title: Refill Order Flow
steps.text: Two-tap refill reorder: confirm address, confirm pouch size, confirm delivery. Pre-filled from registration data. Every friction point from the reorder decision is removed before the user feels it.

steps.title: Subscribe & Save Setup
steps.text: After the first refill, users are prompted to set a recurring delivery. They choose their cadence — 4, 6, or 8 weeks — and lock in a 15% loyalty discount that compounds the more consistently they refill.

steps.title: Sustainability Impact Dashboard
steps.text: A live counter shows each user their personal environmental contribution: plastic bottles avoided, grams of plastic not produced, and carbon offset estimate. Makes eco-behaviour feel visible, rewarding, and worth sharing.

steps.title: Community & Skin Tips
steps.text: Users who refill twice unlock a skin-tips module with dermatologist-approved guidance for their specific skin type. Creates a non-commercial reason to return to the QR experience beyond the transaction.

content.text: 11. Core Product Loops

items: Behavior Loop — Premium packaging changes placement and intentional use → routine integration improves → consistent use drives visible results → trust in the formula deepens into habit.
Refill Loop — Level indicator spotted or smart prompt received → QR scan triggers reorder → pouch delivered → bottle refilled → user never runs out → repurchase happens without conscious effort.
Sustainability Loop — Refill purchased → plastic-saved counter updates → user sees their impact → shares it → friends adopt the same system → brand equity grows organically through advocacy.

Loyalty Loop — First purchase → QR activation → refill subscription → loyalty discount locked in → routine ownership established → Cetaphil becomes a long-term skincare system, not a repeat transaction.

content.text: 12. MVP: What to Build First

The MVP is not the full refill system. It is the minimal proof that the behavior hypothesis is correct. Can better packaging change how users engage with the product? Start with the redesigned bottle and the QR digital touchpoint. Validate refill intent and usage behavior before building the pouch supply chain and subscription infrastructure.

content.text: 13. Feature Prioritization

items: P0 — Must have for MVP: Redesigned bottle silhouette, airless pump, travel lock, QR code on bottle, landing page, skin setup flow, refill prompt, and 2-tap refill order.
P1 — Build next: Matte soft-touch finish, subscribe-and-save subscription flow, sustainability impact counter, and pastel variant trial edition.
P2 — Future roadmap: Refill pouch supply chain at scale, loyalty rewards module, skin tips content library, social sharing mechanic, and community UGC loop.
Out of scope for v1.0: Native app development, in-store digital integration, personalised formula variants, AI skin analysis, and international refill logistics.

content.text: 14. North Star Metric & Supporting Metrics

content.north-star-why: If a user subscribes to refill pouches, three things are confirmed: the bottle is premium enough to keep, the formula is trusted enough to repurchase, and Cetaphil has entered their long-term routine — not just their bathroom shelf. Every downstream metric flows from this one signal.

content.text: 15. GTM Strategy: 5 Phases

phases.title: Pilot Research
phases.text: Test the new bottle design with 500 loyal Cetaphil users. Core questions: Does the premium feel change how they store and use the product? Does the airless pump reduce spills? Does the refill concept excite or confuse? Gather behavioral data before any public launch.

phases.title: Premium Bottle Launch
phases.text: Launch the redesigned bottle as the Cetaphil Skin System. Position it as the same trusted formula in a packaging system designed for a deliberate, intentional skincare routine. Activate the QR digital experience on day one of launch.

phases.title: Refill System Launch
phases.text: Introduce refill pouches as the sustainable, smart repurchase option. Subscribe-and-save goes live. Sustainability counter activates. The refill loop becomes the product's biggest retention mechanic and competitive differentiator.

phases.title: Campaign — Not Handwash
phases.text: Creators receive the new bottle and document the difference. 'I've been using Cetaphil for years but it felt like utility until now.' The Not Handwash campaign makes the perception shift visible, relatable, and shareable. The hashtag becomes the social proof engine.

phases.title: Community & Scale
phases.text: Users share their sustainability counter stats. The plastic-saved community metric becomes a collective milestone. Pastel variant editions drive gifting behavior. The refill system scales and becomes Cetaphil's primary repurchase channel and brand loyalty story.

content.label: Campaign Platform — Not Handwash
content.headline: It has been there all along. You just never treated it like skincare.
examples: This is not handwash. This is the cleanser that dermatologists actually recommend.
You placed it next to the soap dispenser. It deserved better.
Same formula. Now in a bottle that looks like skincare — because it is.
Your skin trusts it. The packaging should too.
Refill it. Keep it. Stop treating your skincare like it is disposable.

content.alt: Cetaphil refill pouch delivered — sustainable subscription concept
content.caption: End state: subscribe, refill, track impact. The routine never breaks and the bottle never goes to landfill.

content.text: 16. PRD Summary

Version 1.0 of the Cetaphil Refill UX System includes: redesigned bottle silhouette with airless pump and travel lock, QR code on every bottle, mobile web experience (no app required) with skin setup, usage guide, and refill order flow, biodegradable refill pouch with subscribe-and-save, and sustainability impact counter. Success criteria for v1.0: 35% QR scan rate among bottle purchasers, 40% first refill order rate, 25% subscribe-and-save conversion, and measurable perception lift in qualitative user research. Out of scope for v1.0: app development, loyalty points system, AI skin analysis, in-store digital integration, and international refill logistics.
17. Risks and Constraints

items: Over-premiumization risk: If the redesign moves Cetaphil too far upmarket, it loses its accessible, dermatologist-trusted identity. The positioning must stay functional-first with premium as the system upgrade, not the lead promise.

Refill complexity risk: If the refill pouch system feels complicated or inconvenient, mainstream buyers will ignore it and revert to buying a new bottle. The UX must make refilling simpler than a new purchase — not harder.

Manufacturing risk: The airless pump and travel lock must be rigorously tested for durability, seal integrity, and cost feasibility before scale. Early failure damages premium perception permanently and is expensive to reverse.

Price sensitivity risk: Any cost increase from the premium redesign must be justified through clear value communication. Cetaphil users skew toward value-for-trust, not luxury skincare pricing — the upgrade must feel earned.

Greenwashing risk: Sustainability claims must be backed by verifiable third-party data. If the plastic-saved counter or biodegradable pouch claims cannot be substantiated, the campaign backfires and actively damages the brand trust that drives everything else.

content.text: 18. Business Impact

The packaging redesign is not a cost center — it is a growth lever. A premium bottle drives counter placement, which drives daily visibility, which drives consistent use. Consistent use drives visible results. Results drive trust, social sharing, and organic referral. The refill system converts one-time buyers into subscribers. Subscribers have predictable lifetime value, lower acquisition cost per repeat purchase, and significantly lower churn than transactional buyers. And the Not Handwash campaign drives earned media through creator content and UGC without requiring large paid distribution budgets. The formula already has trust. The system earns loyalty.
19. PM Reasoning

As a PM working on this problem, the instinct is not to redesign the bottle because it looks better. The instinct is to change the behavior the bottle produces. Packaging is a behavioral input. It shapes where users place the product, how often they reach for it, how they feel when they use it, whether they take it while traveling, and whether they bother to refill it or just buy a new one. Every one of those behaviors has a downstream metric: daily active use, product retention, travel-use conversion, repeat purchase rate, and subscription lifetime value. This strategy starts with the behavioral question — what would users do differently if the packaging reflected the quality of what is inside? — and designs the system backward from that answer.
The formula has already earned trust. The packaging should make people behave like it is worth trusting.
20. Final Conclusion

Cetaphil's next opportunity is not in the formula. The formula is credible. The opportunity is in the full product system that surrounds the formula — the packaging, the refill loop, the digital touchpoint, and the brand story that ties them together. Not Handwash is not just a campaign line. It is a strategic reframe. It positions Cetaphil from a utility cleanser in a basic bottle to a dermatologist-trusted skincare system in packaging designed for intention, travel, refill, and routine. When the packaging matches the formula, the behavior follows.
The reel closes with a consumer-research prompt: Has packaging ever stopped you from buying something you actually needed? Drop the brand below — and that comment section becomes the next episode.

content.text: Otrivin gives fast relief. But nobody tracks how many days they have been using it. That gap is the strategy.

This is the complete strategy behind Episode 03 of #IFIRANTHEBRAND. The reel frames the question in 60 seconds — why does a trusted OTC brand have no system for responsible usage? This case study unpacks the product-management answer: the behavioral problem behind nasal spray misuse, the insight that makes Naak Ki Diary the right solution, and how a simple WhatsApp-led experience turns Otrivin from a reactive relief product into India's nasal health companion.
1. Executive Summary

Otrivin is a trusted OTC nasal decongestant. The product solves an urgent problem: blocked nose. But the bigger opportunity is not just relief — it is responsible usage. Users do not track how many days they have been using nasal spray. They do not know when to stop. They do not know when to see a doctor. Naak Ki Diary is a WhatsApp-led nasal health behavior system that changes this. Users scan a QR code, answer 5 quick questions in Hinglish, receive a personalized Naak Score, take a responsible-use pledge, get check-ins every 3 days, and receive doctor referral support if repeated usage crosses a risk threshold. The strategy turns Otrivin from a transactional relief brand into India's nasal health authority.

content.label: Core PM Insight
content.text: People don't track nasal health until it becomes a problem. The relief moment is the only moment they engage with the brand — and that is exactly where the behavior intervention needs to happen.
2. The Problem

Otrivin is remembered at the moment of blockage — and forgotten at the moment of responsibility. Most users treat a blocked nose as a small inconvenience. They use the spray, feel relief, and move on. They do not track how many days they have used it. They do not know when usage becomes risky. And they have no reason to return to the brand until the next episode of congestion. The product problem is not awareness. It is behavior after purchase. Otrivin has strong top-of-mind recall for relief but near-zero engagement with the responsible-use story that could make it a trusted long-term health brand.
3. User Pain Points

content.label: Real words from real users
voices: Meri naak baar baar band ho jaati hai — I just spray and forget about it.
Spray ke bina neend nahi aati. I don't know how long this has been happening.
Mujhe nahi pata kitne din se use kar raha hoon. 2 weeks? 3 maybe?
I thought the blocking was seasonal. Turns out my spray habit made it worse.
Nobody told me there was a limit. I assumed more spray means faster relief.

content.text: 4. Target Users

users.title: The Frequent Spray User
traits: Uses nasal spray multiple times a week without tracking days
Spray ke bina neend nahi aati — dependency forming gradually without awareness
Does not associate prolonged use with any kind of risk
Only remembers Otrivin when blocked, never when managing nasal health
Needs a simple, non-scary way to understand whether their behavior is safe

users.title: The Pollution-Affected Urban User
traits: Faces blocked nose, sneezing, and dryness due to high AQI or seasonal change
Confused between relief and prevention — uses spray for both without distinction
Wants to know whether congestion is pollution-triggered, habitual, or chronic
Responds to city-specific, contextually relevant nasal health messaging
Would use a daily nasal hygiene product if guided correctly by the brand

users.title: The Chemist Buyer
traits: Buys Otrivin at a chemist shop when the problem is already fully active
Does not read long product instructions at the point of purchase
Needs a behavior intervention at the exact moment of buying, not after
Low friction is non-negotiable — a QR scan is the limit of acceptable effort
Most likely to complete a 5-question check if it begins immediately after purchase

content.text: 5. Strategic Reframe
Most nasal spray campaigns say: blocked nose? Use Otrivin. This strategy says: blocked nose? Understand your naak first.

That single shift moves Otrivin from a reactive relief brand to a nasal health authority. The current brand role is transactional — use it when blocked, buy it at the chemist. The proposed brand role is relational — a companion that helps users understand their nasal behavior, use products responsibly, and know when to seek help. This is not a smaller campaign idea. It is a category leadership position that no OTC nasal brand in India currently owns.
6. The Product Concept: Naak Ki Diary

Naak Ki Diary is a WhatsApp-based nasal health diary. Users scan a QR code — on the Otrivin box, a chemist counter, a college mirror, or an Instagram story. WhatsApp opens directly. No app download. No registration form. The bot asks 5 questions in Hinglish, generates a personalized Naak Score, invites the user to take a 3-day responsible-use pledge, and checks in every 3 days. If the user reports prolonged usage, the bot offers doctor referral. The entire experience runs inside WhatsApp — already a daily behavior platform for over 500 million Indians — which means zero adoption friction.
7. WhatsApp Bot User Journey

steps.title: QR Scan Trigger
steps.text: User scans QR on Otrivin box, chemist counter, college mirror, desk card, or Instagram story. WhatsApp opens directly — zero friction, no app download, no form required.

steps.title: WhatsApp Bot Welcome
steps.text: Bot says: Hi, main hoon Naak Ki Diary. 5 sawaal mein bataata hoon tumhari naak ka haal. Tayaar ho? Warm, immediate, Hinglish — not clinical.

steps.title: 5-Question Nasal Health Check
steps.text: Pichle hafte kitne din naak band rahi? Spray use kiya? Subah khud khulti hai? Raat mein neend tooti? Aaj kitni baar chhink aaye? Quick-tap answers.

steps.title: Naak Score Generated
steps.text: Personalized score out of 100 with status label, city AQI context, and a tailored recommendation. The score card is visual, shareable, and specific to the user's actual answers.

steps.title: 3-Day Responsible Use Pledge
steps.text: Bot asks: 3 Din Pledge loge? Reply HAAN. User commits to responsible usage. A public commitment that raises behavioral accountability beyond the moment.

steps.title: Public Pledge Wall
steps.text: After pledging, the user's first name and city appear on naakkidiary.in. Rahul from Delhi joined 14,208 Indians pledging responsible nasal spray use.

steps.title: 3-Day Check-In Loop
steps.text: Bot checks in every 3 days: Rahul, naak kaisi hai aaj? 3 din ho gaye. Update do. Creates retention without paid media and keeps Otrivin top-of-mind with purpose.

steps.title: Doctor Referral Trigger
steps.text: If the user reports 7+ consecutive days of nasal spray use in check-ins, the bot offers a doctor referral. Your nose needs a doctor, not more spray. Triggered by behavior, not score alone.

content.text: 8. Naak Score System

steps.title: Naak Champion
steps.text: Nasal health behavior is on track. Bot tone: celebrate and reinforce. Recommendation: continue current routine, consider Breathe Clean as a daily preventive nasal hygiene habit.

steps.title: Warning Zone
steps.text: Usage pattern needs attention. Bot tone: gentle nudge without alarm. Recommendation: track usage days more carefully, try nasal rinse for high-AQI pollution days.

steps.title: Naak Ka Nasha — Stage 1
steps.text: Spray overuse patterns detected. Bot tone: warm correction with a nasal hygiene suggestion. Recommendation: stop spray, switch to daily nasal hygiene support, track for 3 days.

steps.title: Naak Ka Nasha — Stage 2
steps.text: Prolonged usage risk detected. Bot tone: serious but caring, never frightening. If 7+ consecutive spray days are reported in check-ins: doctor referral triggered automatically.

content.text: 9. Campaign Copy: The Bot Speaks Hinglish

content.label: WhatsApp Bot Voice
content.headline: Naak check karo. Spray responsibly. Breathe better.
examples: 5 sawaal. 1 Naak Score. Shuru karte hain?
Rahul, naak kaisi hai aaj? 3 din ho gaye. Update do.
Your nose needs a doctor, not more spray.
Mujhe pata hi nahi tha ki main spray itna use kar raha tha — that is the insight this campaign surfaces.
Main Otrivin sirf recommended duration ke andar use karunga. Symptoms bade toh doctor se milunga. Reply HAAN.

content.text: 10. Core Product Features

items: WhatsApp Bot — The core engine. Zero app downloads. Accessible to every age group. QR entry from box, chemist, college, corporate, or society WhatsApp group.
Naak Score — Personalized 5-question health check with 4 score levels, city AQI context, and a shareable visual card that feels like a Spotify Wrapped for nasal health.
3-Day Pledge — Public commitment that raises accountability and adds the user to the naakkidiary.in pledge wall with explicit consent.
Check-In Loop — Automated 3-day WhatsApp follow-up that creates retention without paid media and keeps Otrivin top-of-mind with behavioral purpose.
Doctor Referral — Usage-triggered (not score-triggered) escalation for users reporting 7+ consecutive spray days. A safety net, not a scare tactic.
India Ka Naak AQI Map — City-wise nasal stress visual on naakkidiary.in based on environmental pollution data. Awareness tool, explicitly not a diagnostic tool.
Naak Stories — YouTube mini-documentary: 4 real people, 4 cities, no actors, no scripts. Humein Pata Nahi Tha. The strongest credibility asset in the campaign.
Otrivin Combo Pack — Fast Relief + Breathe Clean at pharmacy shelf. Relief when blocked. Daily nasal hygiene after. Makes the responsible journey physical.

The MVP is the WhatsApp bot plus QR entry plus shareable score card. No website, no app, no AQI map in version 1.0. The validation question is simple: will users complete a 5-question check and take a pledge inside WhatsApp? Prove that before building the full ecosystem.

content.text: 12. Feature Prioritization

items: P0 — Must have for MVP: WhatsApp bot entry via QR and keyword, 5-question health check, Naak Score generation, shareable score card, responsible-use pledge, 3-day check-in loop, and usage-triggered doctor referral message.
P1 — Build next: Public pledge wall on naakkidiary.in, city AQI integration, Instagram story sharing mechanic, chemist QR stickers at counter, basic bot analytics dashboard.

P2 — Future roadmap: College campus Naak Ka Aayna mirror activation, corporate 18-Degree-Problem desk drops, residential society WhatsApp AQI alerts, YouTube Naak Stories documentary, Otrivin Combo Pack at pharmacy shelf.
Out of scope for v1.0: Native app, Practo API live integration, personalised AQI-to-user health matching, cross-brand mask collaboration, ENT clinic network tie-ups.

content.text: 13. North Star Metric & Supporting Metrics

content.north-star-why: The goal is not QR scans. The goal is behavior change. If a user completes the Naak Score, takes the pledge, and responds to the 3-day check-in, all three things are confirmed: they understood the risk, they committed to responsible use, and they came back. That three-step loop is the only signal that the strategy is actually working.

content.text: 14. Go-To-Market: 6 Phases

phases.title: WhatsApp MVP Pilot
phases.text: Launch with QR codes on digital posts and a small selection of chemist counters. Core validation question: do users complete the 5-question check and take the pledge? Measure bot completion and check-in response rate before any wider rollout.

phases.title: Chemist QR Rollout
phases.text: Place QR stickers on all Otrivin boxes and chemist shop counters. This is the highest-intent touchpoint in the system — the user is actively buying relief. The message at the counter: Naak band hai? Pehle Naak Score check karo.

phases.title: Website Hub Launch
phases.text: Launch naakkidiary.in with India Ka Naak AQI Map, the public pledge wall, Naak Stories, and daily nasal stress updates by city. The website turns the campaign from a brand activation into a public health movement with a permanent digital home.

phases.title: Social Sharing Campaign
phases.text: Launch the #NaakKiDiary score card campaign on Instagram. Users share their personalized Naak Score cards. Otrivin reposts selected cards. The shareable output creates UGC without incentivization — personal scores feel specific, relatable, and worth sharing.

phases.title: Offline Activations
phases.text: College campuses get Naak Ka Aayna — a mirror installation with QR and the prompt: Dekho toh sahi — naak theek hai? Corporate offices get 18-Degree-Problem desk cards. Residential societies get daily AQI nasal stress alerts in society WhatsApp groups. Each touchpoint drives one action: a QR scan into the bot.

phases.title: Product + Trade Layer
phases.text: Launch Otrivin Combo Pack — Fast Relief plus Breathe Clean — at the pharmacy shelf. Message: Fast relief when blocked. Daily nasal hygiene after. The combo pack makes the responsible usage journey physical and gives the chemist a stronger basket upsell.

content.text: 15. Regulatory and Risk Thinking

items: Campaign framing risk: Never position this as anti-product or anti-usage. Frame it as responsible use education — Otrivin is the brand that helps users use nasal relief correctly, not the brand that tells them to stop buying.

Medical claim risk: Avoid all cure language across every touchpoint. Use awareness, prevention, and safe-use education language only. All messaging must comply with the Drugs and Cosmetics Act and UCPMP 2024 OTC communication rules.

Bot drop-off risk: If the bot journey feels long or clinical, users will exit before completing the score. Keep it to 5 questions only. Hinglish tone, quick-tap options, and an instant score reward are the drop-off prevention mechanisms.

Doctor referral complexity: Do not build Practo API integration in version 1.0. Start with an informational message only — Consult a doctor. Test actual live referral integration in Phase 2 with a small, measurable sample group.
Pledge wall privacy risk: Show only first name and city. Require explicit consent before any name appears publicly. Make the opt-out as simple and visible as the opt-in.

AQI diagnostic misunderstanding risk: The AQI map must be clearly labeled as an environmental nasal stress awareness tool — not a diagnostic tool. Required disclaimer on every touchpoint: This is not medical advice. Consult a doctor if symptoms persist.

content.text: 16. Why This Is a PM Case Study

A normal campaign for Otrivin says: blocked nose? Fast relief. That is a product message, not a product strategy. This case study treats the problem as a PM would — what is the real user behavior, what creates the gap, and what system closes it? Naak Ki Diary includes user acquisition through QR, WhatsApp onboarding, health behavior scoring, personalized feedback, shareable outputs, habit check-ins, risk-based doctor escalation, public commitment mechanics, offline-to-digital conversion, product bundling, retention loops, and category positioning. Every element maps to a specific metric, a specific user story, and a specific product decision. That is what separates a PM case study from a creative brief.
Otrivin didn't just sell relief. It started India's conversation about nasal health.

content.text: This is the complete strategy page for a reel-style episode. The focus is how Zudio could use its affordability and trend speed to build a stronger digital relationship with young shoppers.
Brand problem

Zudio has high offline buzz, but the digital brand experience can become more intentional. Many shoppers discover products through store visits and social chatter, but the brand could create a stronger repeat loop before and after the visit.
Customer insight
Young value-fashion shoppers want novelty, low-risk experimentation, and social proof. They want to know what is new, what is worth visiting for, and how others are styling affordable finds.
Proposed strategy

items: Launch weekly city-wise trend drops that make store visits feel timely.
Build a UGC loop around styling challenges and affordable outfit formulas.
Create a simple store-discovery content format: what to look for this week.
Use creator micro-collabs to make new arrivals feel more visible and aspirational.

content.text: Expected impact
The strategy can increase store intent, repeat visits, organic creator content, and brand love without losing Zudio's accessible positioning.

content.text: This episode format is designed for brands where the reel introduces the strategic angle and the website carries the complete thinking.
Brand problem
Skincare is crowded, trust-heavy, and full of similar claims. A new D2C brand cannot win only by saying clean, effective, or dermatologist-backed. It needs a sharper wedge.
Customer insight
Customers are tired of overpromising. They want routines that feel understandable, proof that feels credible, and content that helps them choose without confusion.
Proposed strategy

items: Own one specific use case instead of trying to be a complete skincare brand on day one.
Turn education into a product funnel: skin concern, ingredient logic, routine fit, proof.
Use before-after content carefully with transparent context and realistic expectations.
Build launch content around decision clarity, not just product aesthetics.

content.text: Expected impact
The goal is stronger trust, clearer differentiation, better content conversion, and a launch story that gives customers a reason to remember the brand.
